chunks: Asim ibn Humayd narrated from Abu Basir from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

"Whoever is unable to perform the expiation that is incumbent upon him, whether by fasting, freeing a slave, or giving charity, in the case of an oath, a vow, or killing, or any other matter requiring expiation, then seeking forgiveness is sufficient as expiation for him, except for the oath of Dhihar (conjugal abstinence), for if he cannot find what to expiate with, it becomes forbidden for him to have sexual intercourse with her, and they are separated, unless the woman consents to remain with him without sexual intercourse."
The Sheikh (may Allah have mercy on him) said: If he divorces her, the expiation falls from him; if he revokes the divorce (re-marries her), it becomes incumbent upon him again.

key_terms.الظِّهَار: A specific form of pre-Islamic and early Islamic conjugal abstinence where a husband declares his wife to his back
key_terms.الْكَفَّارَةُ: Expiation or compensation for a religious obligation or sin
key_terms.رَاجَعَهَا: He revoked the divorce and took her back

ai.seo_question: What is the expiation for an oath of Dhihar if one cannot afford the standard penalty?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi records this ruling in *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, highlighting the flexibility of Shia jurisprudence where *istighfar* (seeking forgiveness) serves as a sufficient substitute for material expiations like fasting or manumission when one is financially unable. The text specifically details the unique case of *Dhihar* (verbal divorce), noting that if the husband cannot afford the required manumission, sexual intercourse is prohibited until the wife consents to a non-sexual cohabitation or he divorces her, thereby dissolving the obligation.
